questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Identify commonly named clay bodies used for pottery.
questions.prompt: A ceramics studio needs a label for the shelf holding prepared clay bodies. Which list belongs on that shelf?
questions.answer: Earthenware body, stoneware body and porcelain body.
questions.explanation: These names describe materials prepared to make different kinds of fired ceramics. The other lists name tools, techniques or finished forms.
options: Earthenware body, stoneware body and porcelain body.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Use observed fired-sample properties to distinguish clay bodies.
questions.prompt: A teacher fires two test pieces according to their suppliers’ instructions and leaves them unglazed. One is porous earthenware. The other is dense stoneware. Explain which sample would usually absorb more water and why. Why should both samples have the same exposure time in a comparison?
questions.answer: The earthenware usually absorbs more water because it has more open pores. The same exposure time gives both samples an equal chance to absorb water.
questions.explanation: Open pores allow water to enter. Keeping the timing equal makes the comparison more informative.

markingGuide.description: Explains water entry through open pores.
Explains how equal exposure time supports comparison.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Select a carving material and tool for a beginner classroom task.
questions.prompt: An art teacher wants pupils to practise making a shallow groove with a blunt modelling tool. Which prepared sample is best for the exercise?
questions.answer: A firm soap tile the tool can mark with light pressure.
questions.explanation: A material that yields under light pressure lets learners control a shallow groove. Stone or hard wood requires tools suited to harder material.
options: A firm soap tile the tool can mark with light pressure.
A strip of hard seasoned wood.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Explain what physical evidence distinguishes an incised carving from a surface mark.
questions.prompt: Two soap tiles have the same curved design. On one tile the line was drawn with washable colour. On the other a pupil removed a thin ribbon of soap along the line. What would you look for under side lighting to identify the carved tile, and why?
questions.answer: Look for a groove below the original surface, which may show a lit edge and a shadow. The groove shows that material was removed along the line.
questions.explanation: Side lighting reveals changes in level. A drawn mark can change colour while the original surface stays level.

markingGuide.description: Identifies a groove or change of surface level.
Explains how side lighting could reveal it.
Connects the groove to removal of material.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Match tie-dye materials to their roles.
questions.prompt: A school group receives plain cotton squares, cotton twine and a teacher-prepared fabric colour bath. Give the role of each material in making a tied resist pattern.
questions.answer: The cotton is the surface to be patterned. The twine binds parts of the cloth so less colour reaches them. The colour bath colours the exposed cloth.
questions.explanation: The pattern depends on where the colour can reach the fabric and where the binding restricts it.

markingGuide.description: Identifies cotton as the fabric to be patterned.
Explains that the twine holds the resist areas tightly.
Explains that the bath supplies colour to exposed fabric.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Plan and produce a small tied-resist textile with deliberate placement.
questions.prompt: Under teacher supervision, mark on a sketch where you want two lighter marks on a cotton square. Bind the corresponding points with twine. Follow your teacher’s directions for colouring and rinsing using a teacher-prepared classroom fabric dye. After untying, compare the cloth with your sketch and describe one match or difference.
questions.answer: A pupil might bind two separate pinches near opposite corners. After colouring, the tied areas should tend to remain lighter. A pupil can point out a match in placement or describe a mark that spread differently from the sketch.
questions.explanation: Planning ties connects an intended pattern with a practical result. Comparing the cloth with the sketch helps identify how the placement and tightness of the ties affected the result.

markingGuide.description: Positions and secures ties in the planned areas.
Completes a dyed sample with identifiable resist marks.
Uses a visible feature to compare the sample with the plan.
